title: World Sjögren's Day: What the Indian Diaspora Should Know About This Underdiagnosed Autoimmune Disease
excerpt: Observed annually on July 23 to mark the birthday of Dr. Henrik Sjögren, World Sjögren's Day highlights a chronic autoimmune condition that affects millions worldwide — many of whom remain undiagnosed for years.
body:
A Disease Hidden in Plain Sight

Every year on July 23, World Sjögren's Day draws attention to one of the most common yet widely misunderstood autoimmune diseases. Created by the Sjögren's Foundation in 2005, the observance falls on the birthday of Dr. Henrik Sjögren, the Swedish ophthalmologist whose 1933 doctoral thesis first described the clinical pattern of dry eyes, dry mouth, and joint pain that came to bear his name.

Sjögren's disease (pronounced SHOW-grins) is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's moisture-producing glands. While dry eyes and dry mouth are the hallmark symptoms, the disease is far more than an inconvenience — it can affect the thyroid, kidneys, liver, lungs, nerves, and joints, making it a systemic condition rather than a localised one.

"The Numbers Tell a Stark Story According to the Sjögren's Foundation, approximately four million Americans live with the disease, and roughly 50% of them are undiagnosed."

The Numbers Tell a Stark Story

According to the Sjögren's Foundation, approximately four million Americans live with the disease, and roughly 50% of them are undiagnosed. About 90% of those affected are women, with onset typically occurring between the ages of 40 and 60, though the condition can appear earlier. It affects approximately one in every 70 people worldwide, according to the International Foundation for Autoimmune and Autoinflammatory Arthritis (IFAA).

Perhaps the most troubling statistic is the diagnostic delay. Patients wait an average of 2.8 years before receiving a correct diagnosis, often cycling through multiple specialists and misdiagnoses. The varied nature of symptoms — which can include fatigue, brain fog, chronic cough, difficulty swallowing, muscle pain, and numbness — means Sjögren's frequently masquerades as other conditions.

Symptoms Beyond Dryness

While dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) are the most recognised symptoms, patients often experience a constellation of other issues. These include blurry vision, light sensitivity, a gritty or burning sensation in the eyes, dry or peeling lips, increased tooth decay, digestive problems, and vaginal dryness. People with Sjögren's also carry a higher risk of developing lymphoma.

The disease can be primary — occurring independently — or secondary, developing alongside another autoimmune condition such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or scleroderma. There is currently no cure, but symptoms can be managed through a combination of artificial tears, saliva substitutes, prescription medications, and lifestyle modifications.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

Autoimmune diseases often receive less attention in South Asian medical communities, where symptoms like dry eyes or fatigue may be attributed to lifestyle factors rather than investigated as signs of an underlying condition. For members of the Indian diaspora, awareness of Sjögren's is particularly important given the potential for delayed diagnosis in communities where autoimmune conditions may carry less public visibility than in Western healthcare settings.

Access to rheumatologists — the specialists who most commonly diagnose and manage Sjögren's — can also be limited in parts of India and among diaspora communities in smaller cities abroad. The Sjögren's Foundation recommends that anyone experiencing persistent dry eyes, dry mouth, or unexplained fatigue combined with joint pain consult a healthcare provider for screening.

How to Participate

World Sjögren's Day activities include fundraising events, social media campaigns using the hashtag #WorldSjogrensDay, virtual education sessions, and community awareness walks. This year, the Sjögren's Foundation continues to advocate for increased research funding and better healthcare access for patients. The foundation's website offers resources for patients and caregivers, including a provider directory and educational materials available in multiple languages.
